title: Skeletal System
shortDescription: Major bones from skull to fibula, the axial/appendicular split, and what the skeleton actually does besides "hold you up".
genZNote: Support. Protect. Move. Three jobs, one scaffold.

illustration.alt: Labelled illustration of the human skeleton showing major bones
illustration.caption: Skeletal System — Cellfie Human Anatomy

structures.name: Skull
structures.description: Bony structure of the head, part of the axial skeleton.
structures.function: Protects the brain and supports the face.

structures.name: Clavicle (collarbone)
structures.description: Long bone connecting the sternum to the shoulder.
structures.function: Supports the shoulder and transmits force from the arm to the trunk skeleton.

structures.name: Rib cage
structures.description: Curved bones enclosing the thoracic cavity, part of the axial skeleton.

structures.name: Vertebral column
structures.description: The spine; part of the axial skeleton.
structures.function: Protects the spinal cord and supports the body's posture.

structures.name: Pelvis
structures.description: Basin-shaped bone structure, part of the appendicular skeleton's girdle.
structures.function: Supports body weight and protects pelvic organs.

structures.name: Humerus
structures.description: Long bone of the upper arm, part of the appendicular skeleton.
structures.function: Forms the shoulder and elbow joints.

structures.name: Radius
structures.description: One of the two forearm bones (thumb side).
structures.function: Works with the ulna to allow forearm rotation.

structures.name: Ulna
structures.description: One of the two forearm bones (pinky side).
structures.function: Forms the main hinge of the elbow joint.

structures.name: Femur
structures.description: The thigh bone; the longest bone in the body.
structures.function: Bears body weight and forms the hip and knee joints.

structures.name: Tibia (shin bone)
structures.description: Larger of the two lower leg bones.
structures.function: Bears most of the body's weight below the knee.

structures.name: Fibula
structures.description: Thinner of the two lower leg bones.
structures.function: Provides muscle attachment and ankle stability, bears little body weight.

comparisons.distinction: Axial skeleton = skull, vertebral column, rib cage (the body's main axis); appendicular skeleton = limbs and their girdles.
A tendon connects muscle to bone; a ligament connects bone to bone.

questions.prompt: In the labelled skeletal illustration, which bone is the longest in the human body?
questions.explanation: The femur (thigh bone) is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
optionNotes: Upper arm bone, shorter than the femur.
Lower leg bone, shorter than the femur.
The thinner lower-leg bone, not the longest.

questions.prompt: Which structure connects muscle to bone?
questions.explanation: A tendon connects muscle to bone; a ligament connects bone to bone.
optionNotes: Connects bone to bone, not muscle to bone.
Cushions joints, doesn't connect muscle to bone.
The membrane covering bone, not a muscle-to-bone connector.

questions.prompt: Which group does the rib cage belong to?
questions.explanation: The rib cage, along with the skull and vertebral column, forms the axial skeleton — the body's central axis.
optionNotes: Appendicular refers to limbs and girdles, not the rib cage.
It is part of the axial skeleton.
The rib cage is bone, part of the skeletal system, not the muscular system.

sections.heading: Major Bones (as labelled)
bullets: Clavicle (collarbone) — connects the arm to the trunk.
Rib cage — protects the heart and lungs.
Vertebral column — protects the spinal cord, supports the trunk.
Pelvis — supports body weight, protects lower organs.
Femur — thigh bone, the longest and strongest bone in the body.
Tibia and fibula — lower leg bones.

rows: Limbs (arms, legs) and their girdles (shoulder, pelvis)
Protects central organs (brain, spinal cord, heart, lungs)

sections.heading: Functions of the Skeleton
bullets: Support — provides the body's structural framework.
Protection — shields vital organs (skull → brain, rib cage → heart/lungs).
Movement — bones act as levers that muscles pull on at joints.
Mineral storage — bones store calcium and phosphate.
Blood cell production — bone marrow produces red blood cells, white blood cells, and platelets.

sections.heading: Joints
sections.body: A joint is where two or more bones meet. Major types include hinge joints (elbow, knee — movement in one plane), ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip — movement in multiple directions), and pivot joints (neck — rotation).

quickRevision.oneLineDefinition: The skeletal system is the bony framework that supports, protects, and enables movement of the body, and also stores minerals and produces blood cells.
keyFacts: Axial skeleton = skull, vertebral column, rib cage; appendicular skeleton = limbs and their girdles.
The femur is the longest and strongest bone in the human body.
Bone marrow produces blood cells — a function often forgotten alongside support/protection/movement.
Radius and ulna are forearm bones; tibia and fibula are their lower-leg equivalents.
commonConfusion: Radius/ulna (forearm) are often mixed up with tibia/fibula (lower leg) since they play analogous roles in different limbs.
"Skeleton protects organs" and "skeleton produces blood cells" are separate functions students often merge into one.

highYieldFacts: The femur is the body's longest and strongest bone.
Bone marrow, not the bone's hard shell, is responsible for blood cell production.
commonTraps: Don't classify the shoulder/pelvic girdles as part of the axial skeleton — they belong to the appendicular skeleton along with the limbs.
Ball-and-socket joints (shoulder, hip) allow far more movement directions than hinge joints (elbow, knee) — don't mix these up in identification questions.
mustRemember: Five functions: support, protection, movement, mineral storage, blood cell production.
Axial = central axis of the body; appendicular = the "appendages" (limbs).
